name: Sport Climbing
tagline: Bolted walls and bold lines — rope, quickdraws, and the redpoint's long courtship.
overview: Sport climbing is roped climbing on protected routes: bolts placed into the rock (or plastic holds on gym walls) catch falls as climbers work moves protected by quickdraws. Its Olympic disciplines are lead (climbing as high as possible on a 15-meter wall in a fixed time), speed (a race up a standardized 15-meter route), and the bouldering branch (see bouldering) — with the combined formats making their Olympic debut at Tokyo 2020 and separating at Paris 2024.

The sport grew from 1970s-80s European climbing (the bolt wars of Verdon and the Frankenjura), through the grade inflation of the 1990s (Adam Ondra's era redefining what was climbable) into the IFSC's world cup circuit (founded 2007) and Olympic recognition. The greats — Lynn Hill's free ascent of The Nose, Tommy Caldwell's Dawn Wall, Janja Garnbret's dominance — sit alongside the gym boom that made climbing one of the fastest-growing activities of the 2020s.

Newcomers should start in a gym with a belay course: climbing's safety system (the belayer's brake hand, the checks, the communication calls) is learned in an evening and practiced forever. Lead climbing comes after top-rope confidence; grading systems (the French sport grades, the Yosemite Decimal System) give the ladder its language.
facts: Modern origins
1970s-80s Europe — the bolting era (Verdon Gorge, Frankenjura) creates sport climbing; Alan Watts-era US development follows
Governing body
International Federation of Sport Climbing (IFSC, 2007, merging the ICC era); world cups and world championships
Olympic history
Tokyo 2020 (combined format: speed, boulder, lead); Paris 2024 (separate speed and combined boulder-and-lead)
The disciplines
Lead (15 m wall, fixed time), speed (standardized 15 m wall, world records near 4.7 seconds), bouldering (see bouldering page)
Grades
French sport grades (7a, 8c) and the YDS (5.10-5.15); the world's hardest routes sit at 9c grade frontiers by climber
Speed records
Samuel Watson and Aleksandra Miroslaw's sub-5-second / sub-6-second era runs
history: Alpinism's crag descendants: free climbing ethics develop (the YDS, the clean-climbing movement after Chouinard's era).
The bolt era: Verdon and the Frankenjura's Sportklettern; Lynn Hill's free ascent of The Nose (1993) caps the movement's legitimacy.
Grade inflation's leap: 9a+ routes, Chris Sharma's era, and the gym boom's beginnings.

Olympic debut (Tokyo's combined) and the Paris split-format era; Janja Garnbret's double golds and the sport's mainstream arrival.
formats: 15-meter routes, one attempt, highest hold counts: the Olympic lead discipline.
The standardized 15-meter wall (IFSC homologated holds, twin lanes): pure sprint climbing.
Paris 2024's format: boulder scores and lead scores multiplied combined into one ranking.
The crag game: redpoints of bolted routes at graded difficulty — the sport's soul.
skills: Footwork & body position
Climbing's real secret: precise feet, hips into the wall, and weight management that saves arms.
Silent-feet drills (climb a route listening for noise); hip-position practice (drop knee, flag); traverse laps focusing only on feet.
Route reading
The pre-climb plan: identifying holds, sequences, and rest positions from the ground.
Flash-reading drills (read, then climb without falls); sequence discussion with partners; memory rehearsal per route.
Lead technique & clipping
The lead game: rope management, clipping positions, and fall psychology.
Clipping practice (quickdraws at height); hang-dog falls (progressive lead falls) with a trusted belayer; no-fall commitment ladders.
Movement vocabulary
The techniques: drop knee, heel hook, toe hook, flag, deadpoint, and dynamic moves (dynos).
Technique circuits (one move-type per session); boulder problems built around each technique; video review monthly.
Finger & pulling strength
The sport's specific strength: hangboard (edge and pocket) work, weighted pulls, and the antagonists' care.
Hangboard protocols (7-on-3-off repeaters, progressive loads); pull-up ladders; antagonist work (push-ups, shoulder bands) to balance.
Redpoint strategy
The project method: working moves, linking sections, and the mental game of the send.
Project-day structure (moves, then links, then full attempts); rest-day discipline; fall analysis journals.
rules: Lead format: climbers attempt a 15 m wall in a fixed time (6 min), highest score by hold (top = 100 by scoring system); falls end the attempt.
Speed: standardized wall, false starts (reaction time checked), single two runs with the faster counting; world records ratified with sensor timing.
Combined (boulder + lead): scores from both disciplines multiplied (Paris 2024 era) into one ranking.
Outdoor ethics: bolted routes climbed from the ground (ground-up redpoint style), falls caught by the belayer, and the leave-no-trace chip-free ethic — route development has its own ethics wars.
Gym rules: belay certification required, checks before every climb, and the gym's grading honesty.
Competition conduct: isolation iso-zone protocols, route viewing periods, and the referees' hold scoring judgments.
Anti-doping applies at IFSC level (WADA code).
equipment: A 60-70 m dynamic rope ($150-300) and a dozen draws ($12-25 each) — the sport's protection system.
Comfortable harness ($50-90) and a belay device (ATC or assisted-braking, $20-90).
The sport's most personal tool ($80-200): beginner comfort first, aggressive down-turned shoes later.
The chalk bag, chalk, and a route brush ($30-50) — gym etiquette includes brushing your marks.
The home training tool ($60-120) — used with discipline (finger injuries are the sport's tax).
training: Climb more than you train: volume on varied routes builds the movement library fastest.
Train fingers carefully: hangboard twice weekly with progressive loads; never hang on injured fingers.
Technique over strength for the first two years: most plateaus are footwork problems.
Antagonist and shoulder work: push-ups, band work, and shoulder prehab keep climbers out of physio.
Rest as training: tendons adapt slower than muscles — the sport's hardest lesson.
pathway: Top-rope certification and the movement ladder (V0-V3, 5.7-5.10).
Lead class, then outdoor trips with experienced partners.
Gym competitions and crag seasons building redpoints.
National championships and the youth world circuit.
The IFSC circuit and the Games' lead, speed, and combined events.

Annual world titles and the circuit's stops (Kranj, Briançon, Chamonix).
The sub-5-second era's sprints on the standard wall.
The world's hardest redpoints (Silence's 9c, the Dawn Wall's free ascent) — climbing's non-competition summit.

name: Bouldering
tagline: Ropeless puzzles on boulders — a few moves, total commitment, crash pads below.
overview: Bouldering is climbing without ropes on problems short enough that a fall is survivable: boulders outdoors (with crash pads and spotters) or walls up to 4.5 meters in gyms. It is climbing distilled to its hardest moves — a handful of maximum-effort sequences called problems, graded by difficulty (the V-scale in the US, Fontainebleau's system in Europe) — and it has become climbing's most popular form thanks to the gym boom.

The discipline's roots run from John Gill's 1950s mathematical approach (the first bouldering specialist) through Fontainebleau's forest culture to the IFSC's world cup series (boulder discipline since 1997-era) and the Olympic stage (part of Tokyo 2020's combined format, and the boulder-and-lead combined at Paris 2024). Janja Garnbret and the Japanese team define the competition era; the outdoor game's peaks are the world's hardest problems (9A/V17 territory).

Newcomers should start at a gym with a belay-free intro: bouldering's entry is immediate (no knots, no partner required), and the etiquette (brush your holds, don't start under other climbers, spot when asked) is simple. Expect forearms to fail before technique does, and expect to be hooked within one session.
facts: Founding era
1950s — John Gill's bouldering specialization (chalk, dynamics, the problem-solving mindset); Fontainebleau's forest tradition parallel
Governing body
IFSC boulder discipline (world cups since 1997 1998-99 era); Olympic combined formats
Grades
V-scale (V0-V17, US) and Fontainebleau grades (3-9A); gym grades usually softer than outdoor
The wall
Gyms: up to 4.5 m with thick flooring; outdoors: boulders with crash pads (typically 2-4 pads per problem)
Olympic status
Tokyo 2020 (combined with speed and lead); Paris 2024 (boulder-and-lead combined)
Competition format
Four problems five problems per round (qualification), scored by tops and zones within time limits
history: John Gill writes bouldering's manifesto: gymnastic movement, chalk, and difficulty as the point.
Fontainebleau's circuit culture and the pebble Sheffield gritstone's headpoint era build the game's outdoor canon.
Crash pads revolutionize the sport; the V-scale (John Sherman's Hueco Tanks system) standardizes grading; gym bouldering begins.

Olympic eras: Tokyo's combined, Paris's boulder-and-lead; the gym boom makes bouldering climbing's biggest branch.
formats: Color-coded problems by grade: the sport's daily bread and its entry point.
Boulders, pads, and spotters: the sport's spiritual home (Fontainebleau, Hueco, Magic Wood).
Timed rounds on 4-5 problems: tops, zones, and attempts scored.
skills: Movement efficiency
Boulder problems are movement puzzles: hip positioning, momentum use, and the minimal-strength solution.
Volume climbing at 60-70% effort; technique-focused circuits (one theme per session); silent climbing drills.
Power moves
The dynamic vocabulary: deadpoints, dynos, and catch momentum moves on bad holds.
Board spray-wall sessions for power; parkour-style jump accuracy work; lag campusing introduced carefully.
Finger strength
The sport's specific engine: hangboard repeaters, limit bouldering, and the injury-prevention discipline.
Hangboard 2× weekly (repeaters: 7 s on, 3 s off); limit boulder sessions (few tries, full rest); antagonist work always.
Reading problems
Beta route reading before pulling on: sequence plans and memory rehearsal.
Flash-attempt discipline (read first); beta-sharing etiquette; memorization games.
Falling & spotting
The safety system: landing technique (feet-first feet and hips together), pad placement, and spotting zones.
Falling drills from increasing heights; pad-placement practice; spotter communication calls.
Project psychology
The outdoor game: working problems over sessions, the frustration management, and the send day.
Project structure (moves, links, sends); rest-day honesty; the tick-list's long game.
rules: Competition scoring: tops (25 points 25 for top, 10 for zone by format) with fewer attempts scoring higher; timed rounds with isolation.
Gym etiquette: brush holds after use, don't start under others, wait rotation discipline at popular problems.
Outdoor ethics: brush ticks off holds, minimize chalk, respect access agreements and seasonal closures (the environment is the gym).
Pads and spotting: enough pads under the line (2-4 typical); spotters guide falls to pads, they do not catch climbers.
Grades: V and Font scales for difficulty; gym grades generally 1-2 a notch softer outdoors; grade your gym honestly.
Combined Olympic format: boulder and lead scores multiplied into one ranking (Paris 2024 rules).

equipment: Aggressive down-turned shoes for hard bouldering ($90-220): the sport's most personal purchase.
For outdoor sessions ($150-300 each; most problems need 2-4).
The hold-brushing tool — gym etiquette and outdoor ethics in one ($10).
training: Volume climbing at moderate effort: 60-90 minute sessions, 2-4× weekly — the movement library compounds.
Limit bouldering weekly: 3-4 tries on projects above your level, with full rest between.
Hangboard twice weekly after six months of base: finger strength arrives on schedule, not sooner.
Antagonists and shoulders every session's end: the injury-prevention tax.

pathway: V0-V2 circuit lapping and the etiquette course.
V3-V6 over the first two years, technique-first.
Citizen competitions and the first Font/Hueco pilgrimages.
National titles and the youth world circuit.
The IFSC boulder circuit and the Games' combined formats.

The season's stops (Meiringen, Salt Lake City, Innsbruck).

name: Mountaineering
tagline: The summit sports — alpinism's mix of climbing, endurance, and mountain judgment.
overview: Mountaineering is the complete mountain sport: rock climbing, snow and ice climbing, glacier travel, navigation, and altitude management combined to ascend peaks — from Alpine classics (the Matterhorn's 1865 first ascent) to the 8000-meter giants (Everest's 1953 first ascent) and the modern alpinism of single-push ascents (Ueli Steck's speed records, Reinhold Messner's oxygenless Everest). It is less a competition than a craft: the summit is the goal, and the descent — where most accidents happen — is the real test.

The sport's institutions run deep: the Alpine Club (1857, the world's first), the UIAA (1932), and the Himalayan Database's records of the 8000ers. Its modern debates — commercial Everest traffic, oxygen use, and the alpine-style ethos vs expedition logistics — are the sport's character questions, and its mountaineers (Messner, the Stecks, the Kaltenbrunners) are judged by style as much as summits.

Newcomers should enter through clubs and courses: mountaineering's safety system (rope work, crevasse rescue, avalanche judgment, weather reading) is taught by mountain guide associations worldwide, and the progression (hiking → scrambling → Alpine PD/AD routes → big mountains) is measured in seasons, not weekends. Fitness, judgment, and patience are the sport's three currencies.
facts: Founding moment
8 August 1786 — Jacques Balmat and Michel-Gabriel Paccard's first ascent of Mont Blanc (4,809 m): alpinism's birth
Governing bodies
UIAA (International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation, 1932); national Alpine Clubs (the AC 1857, the AAC, the CAI); IFMGA guide associations
The 8000ers
Fourteen peaks above 8,000 m: Everest (8,849 m) first ascended 1953 (Hillary and Norgay); all fourteen completed by 1986 (Messner)
Grading systems
The Alpine grading system (F, PD, AD, D, TD, ED), the IFAS ice scale, and route-specific grading
Disciplines
Alpine style (light, fast, self-sufficient), expedition style (fixed ropes, camps), ski mountaineering's cousin branch
Safety reality
Descents and objective hazards (avalanche, rockfall, weather) cause most accidents — judgment is the sport's core skill
history: The Alpine golden age begins: Mont Blanc's first ascent, the Alpine Club's founding (1857), and the great first ascents (the Matterhorn, 1865, with the Whymper tragedy).
The Alps' last problems fall; the Himalaya's reconnaissance era; the 8000ers' first attempts.
Annapurna's first 8000er (Herzog, 1950) and Everest's first ascent (Hillary and Norgay, 1953): the great expedition era peaks.
The alpine-style revolution: Messner and Habeler's oxygenless Everest (1978), Messner's solo Everest (1980), and the all-fourteen completion (1986).
Commercial Everest's growth; the speed-alpinism era (Ueli Steck's Eiger records); K2's winter first ascent (Nims Purja's project era).
The 14-peaks speed records (Purja's six months), winter 8000er completions, and the sport's climate-change-era reckoning.
formats: Single-push, light-and-fast ascents of Alpine-scale routes: the purist discipline.
The big mountains' logistics: camps, fixed ropes, and Sherpa-supported team-supported ascents.
The skin-and-ski ascents (see ski mountaineering within winter pages cross-country and skimo): the winter branch.
The protected and walking entries into mountain terrain: every alpinist's start.
skills: Movement on mixed terrain
Rock, snow, and ice movement: crampon technique, ice axe use, and the mountain walker's scrambler's balance.
Crampon technique courses (flat-footing, front-pointing); ice axe self-arrest drills (learned on slopes); scrambling with mentorship.
Rope work & glacier travel
The safety system: roped glacier travel, crevasse rescue, and belayed climbing on ridges.
Crevasse-rescue courses (practiced annually); rope-team drills; prusik hauling systems rehearsed until automatic.
Navigation & weather judgment
The mountain's map: compass and GPS navigation, weather-reading, and the turnaround discipline.
Navigation courses; weather-forecast literacy (mountain forecasts read daily); turnaround times set and honored.
Altitude management
The body's altitude project: acclimatization schedules, hydration, and AMS/HACE/HAPE recognition.
Climb high, sleep low protocols; symptom knowledge (headache, ataxia, breath); gradual gain rates (300-500 m sleep-gain above 3,000 m).
Avalanche & objective hazard
The winter mountain's law: terrain assessment, snowpack basics, and the decision frameworks (avalanche problem types).
AIARE-style avalanche courses; terrain-choice practice; the human-factor training (the heuristics that kill).
Expedition craft
The big mountains' logistics: fitness, nutrition, gear systems, and the Sherpa-partnership ethics.
Load-carriage training (rucking with pack weight); expedition nutrition planning; camp skills (melting, shelter) practiced.
rules: No competition rules — mountaineering is governed by judgment: the weather, the mountain's condition, and the team's honesty are the referee.
The style debate: alpine style (self-sufficient pushes) versus expedition style (camps and fixed ropes) — the sport's ethical spectrum (Messner's essays define the vocabulary).
Guiding and qualifications: IFMGA guides carry the profession's standard; clients' responsibilities are defined by guide associations.
Access and ethics: permits (national park systems, Himalayan royalties), Leave No Trace, and the fixed-rope human-waste debates of the commercial era.
Rescue: self-sufficiency expected; helicopter rescue where available is emergency infrastructure, not a plan.
Environmental duty: the mountains' climate change is visible from base camp — the sport's modern stewardship conversations.
Insurance and medical: high-altitude insurance and evacuation coverage are expedition requirements.
equipment: The mountain's clothing science: base, insulation, and shell layers by mountain ($500-1,500 the system).
Mountaineering boots (B2-B3 by grade) with crampons ($300-900 together).
Ice axe, rope (60 m), slings, and hardware ($300-600 the basic rack).
GPS, maps, altimeter, and satellite communicator (inReach-class, $300-400): the modern safety layer.
Sleeping system, shelter, stove, and the altitude pharmacy (Diamox prescriptions by doctor): the big-mountain list.
training: Build the aerobic engine: rucking (weighted hiking), stair climbs, and long endurance days — mountaineering is an aerobic sport.
Practice the skills annually: self-arrest, crevasse rescue, and navigation drift without rehearsal.
Train altitude gradually: graduated altitude gains, hydration discipline, and honest symptom tracking.
Strength for the pack: legs and core for load carriage; the downhill strength matters as much as up.
Learn judgment deliberately: debrief every objective-hazard decision with your team — the sport's real curriculum.
pathway: Mountain walking and grade-1 scrambles with clubs.
Glacier school, avalanche courses, and self-arrest training.
Guided or club-led Alpine classics building experience.
Aconcagua, Denali, then the 8000ers (commercial or independent by style).
Alpine-style firsts, winter ascents, and speed records — the sport's cutting edge.
events: Everest (1953) through Shishapangma's completion and the winter ascents (K2's 2021 first winter ascent).
Ueli Steck's Eiger north face records (2:47) and the modern timed ascents.
Mountaineering's most prestigious honor: the year's finest ascents by style.
Club meets and the membership's shared seasons.
The skimo world cup's Olympic arrival (Milan-Cortina 2026) — the sport's competitive branch.

Italy — the sport's philosophical revolutionary: oxygenless Everest, the solo Everest, and all fourteen 8000ers.
Ueli Steck

getting_started: Join an Alpine Club or hiking group: the community teaches what books cannot.
Take a glacier or mountaineering course within your first year: self-arrest and crevasse rescue are mandatory literacy.
Build the aerobic base with weighted hiking: the sport's fitness is walking uphill with a heavy pack.
Start with guided Alpine routes (PD grade): the mentorship buys seasons of experience safely.
Read the classics (Into Thin Air, The White Spider, Annapurna): the sport's judgment is taught through its stories.
Respect the turnaround: the summit is optional; the descent is mandatory.
glossary: Light, fast, self-sufficient climbing — no camps hanging on the route.
The body's altitude adaptation: climb high, sleep low.
Stopping a slide with the ice axe — the sport's first safety skill.
The glacier's crack: roped travel exists because of it.

name: Orienteering
tagline: The thought sport — map, compass, and the fastest route nobody else can find.
overview: Orienteering is racing with a map and compass: competitors navigate point-to-point through checkpoints (controls) over unknown terrain, choosing their own routes between them — running as fast as they can think. The classic formats are foot-O (forest courses of 3-15 km), sprint-O (urban park courses at mile race pace), ski-O, and mountain-bike-O, all governed by the International Orienteering Federation (IOF) with world championships and a World Cup series.

Born from Scandinavian military land-navigation training (the first public competition in Norway, 1897), the sport became Sweden's and Finland's civic obsession — the O-Ringen's five-day festival draws thousands — and spread to 80+ nations. Its champions (Thierry Gueorgiou's 14 multiple world titles, Tove Alexandersson's modern dominance) are navigation artists: the sport's elite train map memory and route-choice logic as deliberately as speed.

Newcomers can start immediately: local clubs put on events with beginner courses (maps provided, instruction included), and the sport's age-graded structure welcomes every speed. The essential skill — keeping the map oriented to the terrain (thumbing the map, checking off features) — is learnable in one afternoon and deepens for a lifetime.
facts: Founding
1897 — the first public competition near Oslo (Norway's military origins); IOF founded 1961 (world championships since 1966)
Governing body
International Orienteering Federation (IOF); national federations (the Swedish and Finnish federations the giants)
Formats
Foot-O (forest, middle/long/relay), sprint-O (urban, knockout sprint world championships since 2018), ski-O, MTB-O, trail-O (precision for all abilities)
The map
IOF-standard maps at 1:4,000-1:15,000 with five-color terrain symbology — regenerated laser-LiDAR era accuracy
The controls
Orange-and-white flags with electronic punching (SportIdent) — the course's proof of visit
The festivals
Sweden's O-Ringen (5 days, thousands), Finland's Jukola relay (the world's biggest night relay), Switzerland's the Swiss O-week
history: Norwegian and Swedish military roots; civilian clubs form; the map-making craft develops.
The IOF's founding and standardized symbols; world championships begin (1966); the sport spreads beyond Scandinavia.
Electronic punching (1990s) transforms the sport; sprint-O's urban growth; the World Cup's professionalization.
The knockout sprint format's arrival (TV-friendly city racing); Tove Alexandersson's era; the sport's laser-map revolution.
formats: Middle (4-6 km), long (10-15 km), and relay formats through forest terrain — the classic discipline.
Urban park and city-center racing at 4 km, winning times 12-15 minutes: the modern TV format.
Winter's and wheels' branches: navigation on skis and bikes.
Headlamp racing and the team formats (Jukola's seven-leg night relay is the sport's Wembley).
skills: Map orientation & thumbing
The core technique: keeping the map turned to the terrain, thumb parked at your position — the sport's constant habit.
Map-walk drills (walk a course keeping the map oriented); thumb map-contact discipline every step; beginner courses with map-in-hand coaching.
Route choice
The strategic layer: comparing lines (trail vs straight), climb costs, and attack-point planning — orienteering's chess.
Route-choice training exercises (plan before each leg); post-race route comparisons; head-to-head analysis at relays.
Compass bearings
Precision navigation across featureless low-visibility terrain: the bearing-and-distance technique.
Bearing drills (short legs, compass only); pacing practice (count double-paces per 100 m); night-O as the graduate school.
Attack points & relocation
The safety system: navigating to a near-the-control feature first, and relocating fast when lost.
Attack-point leg design in training; stop-and-relocate drills (deliberate planned confusion); the five-second pause-and-look habit.
Running speed & terrain fitness
The sport's engine: running fast on rough ground, uphill-downhill strength, and the map-under-fatigue discipline.
Terrain running 2× weekly; hill strength (uphill repeats); map-sprint simulations (hard running, hard thinking).
Sprint-O technique
The urban game: reading complex multi-level maps (stairs, passages, canopies) at race pace.
Sprint-map training in cities; passable barrier passage symbols mastered; knockout-sprint heat practice.
rules: Course: controls visited in numbered order; electronic punching proves the visit; the fastest total time wins.
Maps: IOF symbology at scale by format (1:4,000 sprint to 1:15,000 forest); out-of-bounds uncrossable features marked and law.
Fairness: no GPS navigation devices (watches logged GPS only for post-race analysis); the map is the only instrument beyond the compass.
Starts: staggered intervals (2-minute starts in forest, mass knockouts in sprint) to prevent following.
Categories by age and gender (from 10 to 95+); elite classes by world-ranking.
The referee's calls: mispunching (missing a control) disqualifies; course boundary violations penalized.
Safety: whistle carried in forest events, emergency checkpoint rescue protocols by organizer; weather holds at the organizer's call.
equipment: Thumb compass (the Nordic choice) or baseplate ($15-60).
Studded orienteering shoes for forest grip ($80-150); trail shoes suffice to start.
Shin gaiters for forest brush ($30-50); a whistle for safety ($5).
The electronic punching card ($40-60; rentals at events).
For night-O (400-800 lumens, $40-120) — the sport's most atmospheric branch.
training: O-technique sessions weekly: one training run where navigation is the workout (slow legs, fast map).
Terrain running: the sport's speed is rough-ground running — train on forest tracks and hills.
Map memory drills: study the map at the start, run the leg from memory where safe.
Race every weekend in season: O-meets are the sport's coaching system.
Winter ski-O or indoor sprint training keeps the navigation brain alive year-round.

name: Paragliding
tagline: Foot-launched flight — thermals, cross-country lines, and the sky as a racecourse.
overview: Paragliding is foot-launched free flight: a ram-air wing (canopy) inflated and launched from slopes or hills, flown by weight-shift and brake inputs, with pilots using rising air (thermals, ridge lift) to stay aloft and fly cross-country courses of 50-300+ km. It is flight's most accessible form — a wing fits in a backpack — and its competition side runs FAI world cups and the X-Alps adventure race's legendary crossing of the Alps by foot and wing.

The sport grew from 1980s parachute-ski experiments in the French and Swiss Alps (the slope-soaring pioneers) into a global free-flight culture: the FAI's World Cup and world championships, the Red Bull X-Alps (since 2003), and a thermal-soaring knowledge base that turns meteorology into a competitive skill. Chrigel Maurer's X-Alps dynasty (ten multiple wins) and the XC league's record flights define the sport's frontier.

Newcomers should take a certified course (national federations' licensing systems): paragliding's safety culture is the sport's real foundation, and the learning ladder (ground handling → small hills → high flights → thermalling → cross-country) is measured in flight hours and conditions judgment. The sport's great truth: the wing is safe; the sky requires reading.

name: Skydiving
tagline: Freefall as a sport — formations, vertical flight, and the canopy's final art.
overview: Skydiving is controlled freefall: jumpers exit aircraft from 3,000-4,500 meters, fly their bodies in freefall (falling at 200 km/h belly-down, or faster in vertical flight modes), deploy canopies around 1,200 meters, and pilot the parachute to a landing. Its competitive disciplines are formation skydiving (teams build scored formations in time), vertical/Freefly (head-down and sit-fly flight), canopy piloting (swooping courses), and accuracy landing — governed internationally by the FAI and nationally by bodies like USPA.

The sport descends from parachute development (André-Jacques Garnerin's 1797 descent from a balloon) through military airborne traditions to the post-war sport culture (the 1950s-60s club era, then the freefall photography and boogie culture). Its modern era: relative work's team precision, the vertical world records (the 164-person large-formation records), wingsuit flying's cousin branch, and a safety record transformed by AADs (automatic activation devices) and square reserves.

Newcomers enter through tandem jumps (instructor-harnessed) and then AFF (Accelerated Freefall) courses: skydiving's licensing ladder (A through D licenses) is standardized and safety-cultured — the sport's training is rigorous because gravity is unforgiving. The community is famously tight; the drop zone is its own world.

name: Drone Racing (FPV)
tagline: First-person view at 150 km/h — video-game reflexes flown through real gates.
origin: 2010s hobbyist era · Drone Racing League 2016 · FAI worlds
overview: Drone racing flies first-person-view (FPV) quadcopters through gated courses at 100-150+ km/h: pilots wear video goggles receiving a live camera feed from the aircraft, flying by sight alone through three-dimensional tracks of gates, flags, and obstacles. The sport fused 2010s hobbyist FPV culture with professional league spectacle — the Drone Racing League (DLR DRL) broadcasts, the FAI's world championships, and the multirotor community's maker culture (every pilot builds, tunes, and repairs their own machine).

The technical stack is the sport's soul: brushless motors, flight controllers running open-source firmware (Betaflight), analog or digital video links, and the pilot's radio — a craft learned as much at the workbench as in the air. The skills are pure hand-eye: 200-millisecond reactions, track memorization, and the simulator-to-real transfer that makes FPV the most training-efficient motorsport (hours in Velocidrone and Liftoff translate directly to gates).

Newcomers should start in the simulator before buying anything: FPV simulators (free to cheap) teach the muscle memory safely, then a beginner build or RTF kit follows. The community is maker-culture warm — local clubs fly micro drones indoors in winter and full-size outdoors in summer, and the progression from tiny-whoop to racing quad takes months, not years.
